body:
Solar energy begins with radiation from the Sun

The Sun emits energy as electromagnetic radiation. A portion of this radiation reaches Earth's surface as sunlight. It can be converted into useful energy in 2 principal ways: photovoltaic technology converts sunlight directly into electricity, while solar thermal technology captures solar radiation as heat.

Solar energy is renewable because sunlight is continuously replenished by the Sun. However, the amount available at a particular place is not constant. It changes with the time of day, season, latitude, cloud cover, atmospheric conditions and orientation of the receiving surface.

Solar irradiance is the rate at which solar radiation delivers energy to a unit area of a surface. Its usual unit is watts per square metre (W/m2).

Irradiance, irradiation and electrical output

Irradiance describes the intensity of sunlight at a particular moment or over a specified short interval. Solar irradiation, also called solar insolation in many resource assessments, is the total solar energy received per unit area during a period. It is commonly expressed in kilowatt-hours per square metre (kWh/m2) per day, month or year.

For example, if irradiance remains at 600 W/m2 for 2 hours, the incident solar energy is 1,200 Wh/m2, or 1.2 kWh/m2. This is the sunlight energy received, not the electricity necessarily produced by a solar panel. Only part of the incident energy can be converted into useful electricity or heat.

QuantityMeaningCommon unit
IrradianceSolar power arriving per unit areaW/m2
IrradiationSolar energy received per unit area over timekWh/m2
PV power outputRate of electrical energy productionW or kW
PV energy outputElectricity generated over a periodWh or kWh

Direct, diffuse and global solar radiation

Sunlight reaching the ground contains different components. These distinctions are important because photovoltaic panels and concentrated solar power plants do not use the components in exactly the same way.

  • Direct beam radiation: Sunlight arriving directly from the visible solar disc without being scattered in the atmosphere.
  • Diffuse radiation: Sunlight scattered by molecules, aerosols, dust and clouds before reaching a surface. It arrives from different directions in the sky.
  • Global radiation: The combined direct and diffuse radiation received by a specified surface.

For a horizontal surface, 3 standard resource terms are particularly useful:

  • Direct Normal Irradiance (DNI): Direct beam irradiance measured on a surface perpendicular to the Sun's rays.
  • Diffuse Horizontal Irradiance (DHI): Diffuse irradiance received by a horizontal surface.
  • Global Horizontal Irradiance (GHI): Total direct and diffuse irradiance received by a horizontal surface.

GHI equals the horizontal component of DNI plus DHI. Therefore, DNI cannot simply be added to DHI without accounting for the angle of sunlight. When the Sun is low in the sky, the same direct beam is spread over a larger horizontal area.

Why solar radiation varies

Solar irradiance is usually higher when the Sun is high in the sky because its rays strike a horizontal surface more directly and travel through less atmosphere. At sunrise and sunset, the rays are more oblique. Earth's rotation produces the daily variation, while the tilt of Earth's axis and its revolution around the Sun produce important seasonal variations.

Clouds commonly reduce direct sunlight and increase the relative importance of diffuse radiation. Dust, haze and atmospheric pollution can also reduce the useful solar resource. Local shadows from trees and buildings reduce the radiation received by an individual installation.

The plane-of-array irradiance is the radiation actually reaching the tilted surface of a solar panel. It is not necessarily equal to GHI because the panel may face a different direction or inclination.

A location with high annual sunshine may still experience large changes in daily electricity production. Solar resource quality must be considered together with the technology used, its orientation and the weather.

Prelims focus

  • Irradiance measures solar power per unit area; irradiation measures accumulated solar energy per unit area.
  • DNI refers to direct sunlight on a surface perpendicular to the solar beam.
  • DHI measures scattered sunlight received on a horizontal surface.
  • GHI includes the horizontal component of direct sunlight and diffuse horizontal irradiance.
  • Clouds and atmospheric scattering affect direct and diffuse radiation differently.
  • Trap: A solar irradiation value in kWh/m2 is not the same as the electricity generated in kWh by a solar panel.

[Sources: NCERT, India: People and Economy, Class 12, chapter 7, Mineral and Energy Resources, p. 82; U.S. Department of Energy, Solar Radiation Basics, sections Types of Solar Radiation and Measuring Solar Radiation, consulted 16 November 2026; National Renewable Energy Laboratory, Best Practices Handbook for the Collection and Use of Solar Resource Data for Solar Energy Applications, 4th edition, September 2024, chapter 2.]

body:
Meaning of the photovoltaic effect

The word photovoltaic combines the ideas of light and electrical voltage. A photovoltaic (PV) cell is a semiconductor device that converts energy from sunlight directly into electrical energy.

A photovoltaic cell does not first produce steam or rotate a turbine. Its electrical output is generated through the interaction of light with a semiconductor. This distinguishes photovoltaic conversion from solar thermal power generation.

Why semiconductors can produce electricity

A semiconductor is a material whose electrical behaviour can be controlled through its composition and structure. Silicon is the most widely used material in conventional solar cells.

A common crystalline-silicon solar cell contains 2 differently treated semiconductor regions:

  • n-type region: Contains electrons as its majority mobile charge carriers.
  • p-type region: Contains holes as its majority mobile charge carriers. A hole represents the absence of an electron in a position where one could otherwise be present.

The boundary between these regions forms a p-n junction. Near this junction, a built-in electric field develops. The field is important because it helps separate the electrical charges produced when the semiconductor absorbs suitable photons.

How sunlight generates electric current

  1. Absorption of photons: Light enters the solar cell. Photons with sufficient energy can be absorbed by the semiconductor.
  2. Generation of charge carriers: Absorption transfers energy to electrons and creates mobile electrons and corresponding holes.
  3. Separation of charges: The electric field associated with the junction helps drive electrons and holes towards different sides of the cell.
  4. Flow through a circuit: When an external conducting path connects the cell's terminals, electrons can move through the circuit and deliver electrical energy to a connected load.

The resulting output is direct current (DC). In DC, charge flows with a consistent direction of conventional current under normal operating conditions. This differs from the alternating current (AC) commonly used in electricity supply networks.

Not every photon is converted into useful electricity. Some light is reflected, some passes through without being absorbed, and some absorbed energy is lost as heat. The cell therefore converts only a fraction of incoming solar energy into electrical energy.

Cell, module and array

A single solar cell is a small electricity-generating unit. Practical systems use many cells together to obtain useful electrical output.

TermMeaningDistinguishing feature
Solar cellIndividual photovoltaic semiconductor deviceBasic unit that converts light into DC electricity
Solar moduleInterconnected cells enclosed in protective materialsManufactured panel unit
Solar panelCommon term for a photovoltaic moduleUsually refers to the visible installed module
Solar arrayGroup of connected photovoltaic modulesProvides the combined output of multiple modules

Common photovoltaic materials

Crystalline-silicon cells are widely used in rooftop and large ground-mounted systems. They are manufactured using silicon crystals. Thin-film photovoltaic cells use very thin layers of semiconductor material deposited on a supporting surface. Both are photovoltaic technologies: the distinction is in materials and manufacturing, not in whether they generate DC electricity.

The electrical output of an individual cell depends on the absorbed sunlight, cell area, semiconductor properties and operating temperature. A larger array can provide more total power because it combines the output of many cells and modules.

Photovoltaic effect: Light creates mobile electrical charges in a semiconductor device, and the device's internal electrical structure enables useful current to flow through an external circuit.

Prelims focus

  • Photovoltaic cells convert sunlight directly into DC electricity.
  • Silicon is a major semiconductor material used in solar cells.
  • The p-n junction helps separate electrons and holes generated by absorbed light.
  • A module contains interconnected cells; an array contains multiple modules.
  • Trap: A photovoltaic cell does not require water heating, steam production or a turbine to generate electricity.

[Sources: U.S. Department of Energy, Solar Photovoltaic Cell Basics, section How Do Photovoltaic Cells Work?, and Solar Photovoltaic Technology Basics, consulted 16 November 2026; NCERT, Resources and Development, Class 8, chapter Mineral and Power Resources, pp. 33–34.]

title: The Photovoltaic Effect: From Sunlight to Direct-Current Electricity

body:
From a photovoltaic module to a useful electricity supply

A photovoltaic module produces DC electricity when sufficient sunlight reaches its cells. To supply common AC appliances or connect to an AC electricity network, a photovoltaic system normally uses an inverter. The inverter converts DC electricity into AC electricity suitable for the intended supply system.

The inverter does not create additional solar energy. It changes the electrical form of the available output, with some energy lost during conversion.

A practical photovoltaic installation may contain modules, mounting structures, an inverter, electrical connections, a meter and, where storage is required, batteries and suitable control equipment. The components present depend on the purpose of the installation.

Utility-scale and rooftop installations

Utility-scale solar PV refers to relatively large installations that generate electricity primarily for delivery to an electricity network. Solar parks commonly contain extensive ground-mounted arrays. Such installations require suitable land, sunlight access and a connection to the power system.

Rooftop solar PV places modules on residential, commercial, institutional or industrial roofs. The generated electricity may serve loads within the building. Where the applicable electricity arrangement permits, surplus generation may be supplied to the grid.

The distinction between rooftop and utility-scale PV is mainly the installation setting and typical scale. Both normally use the same basic photovoltaic principle.

Grid-connected, off-grid and hybrid systems

Another classification concerns how electricity is supplied and whether a utility grid is available.

SystemConnectionTypical application
Grid-connected PVOperates in coordination with an electricity gridRooftops and utility-scale solar plants
Off-grid PVOperates without relying on a utility-grid connectionRemote homes, lighting and water pumps
Hybrid or storage-backed PVCombines PV with batteries and may also connect to the gridSupply extending beyond sunlight hours or during selected outages

An off-grid system may use electricity directly during sunny hours. Where electricity is needed at night or when sunlight is inadequate, it commonly incorporates battery storage or another dependable supply source. For example, a solar-powered irrigation pump may operate during daylight without requiring a battery for night-time operation.

A battery stores electrical energy supplied by the PV system for later use. Battery storage increases the ability to supply electricity at times when solar generation is low, but it does not make the photovoltaic cells generate electricity in darkness.

Most ordinary grid-connected rooftop PV systems without specially configured backup capability stop supplying power during a grid outage, even if sunlight is available. A system designed for backup supply needs appropriate equipment and operating arrangements. Therefore, having rooftop panels alone does not guarantee electricity during a power cut.

Typical applications

  • Homes and public buildings: Rooftop generation for lighting, fans, appliances and other suitable electrical loads.
  • Industry: Electricity for industrial and commercial electrical consumption.
  • Agriculture: Solar-powered pumping of water where daytime operation is suitable.
  • Remote locations: Electricity for communication equipment, small facilities and lighting where extending the grid may be difficult.
  • Electricity networks: Large solar installations contributing generation to the grid.

The selection of a system depends on access to sunlight, the timing of electricity demand, grid availability and whether storage is needed.

Prelims focus

  • PV modules generate DC electricity; an inverter converts DC into AC.
  • Rooftop and utility-scale describe installation setting and scale.
  • Grid-connected and off-grid describe the relationship with the electricity network.
  • Off-grid solar pumping can use electricity directly during daylight.
  • Batteries store energy for later use; they do not produce solar energy.
  • Trap: A grid-connected solar rooftop does not automatically provide backup electricity when the grid fails.

[Sources: U.S. Department of Energy, Solar Photovoltaic System Design Basics, sections Inverters, Mounting Structures and Storage, consulted 16 November 2026; NCERT, Resources and Development, Class 8, chapter Mineral and Power Resources, pp. 33–34.]
